inventions: Thornwater in the days after the ford: Cael's calf measured in paces (eleven flat, nine uphill, twelve downhill) as the chapter's cataloguing spine; a morning inventory at the loft ladder; Lira's stick cut from a hay-fork handle by Seln; the steading's woman's re-binding of Brom's arm and her two verdicts on Lira's ankle ('It'll set how it sets'; 'It'll set stiffer').

The field library: the steading's harvest bread-table (a plank on trestles at the barn's end) lent to Karis; the boxes' contents catalogued (bundled copies with subject slips, a folding rule, chalk, a pencil tin, two bound books); the bundles stood on end as shelves; Karis's one-page 'shelf' of edge-territory lore (the ford lore, dictated) as the only source she owns from this side of the Line.

The grain moving on the fifth day after the ford: six carts up from Lowmarch, two driven by carters' wives; Karis questioning every carter about the void roads (which roads, where they go); a man with a clouded eye who 'did not talk about roads to paper'; the carter's wife as a woman of forty in an oversized coat with a boy of ten on the board — unnamed, three sentences only, gone in the next cart-length.

The road back as a grain convoy: the boxes roped on the second cart, Lira on the lead cart's tail by her own declared decision, the stretch crossed at noon with carters talking through it, a ring-camp above the wash with a carters' fire; Brom re-binding his own arm one-handed with his teeth while Cael holds the loose end unasked.

Lira's Norhold beat given a small mechanism: 'they wrote it in the column for things people say'; the bracket described as rungs with numbers and a panel at the top of each flight; Brom's one-word answer ('Fast') and her rejection of it ('Fast was the floor').

Lowmarch on the sixtieth day: fourteen slips (the ford, the autumn road, and the grain escort gone; two escorts, a fence-line, and a four-mark well-clearing added); Seln taking the well by moving the slip a quarter-inch; Pike's line that the ford was read at the plank a week ago and the saying would be done that night at the book with the crew present.

Brom's question overheard by Cael from the plank's far end (Brom flattens rather than lowers his voice; Pike answers at his pitch regardless); Brom borrowing Cael's pencil and one of Pike's old carter-slips to write the eight words, folded inside his shirt; Pike's follow-on lines about his own Copper paper ('I stopped carrying the paper the second year, because it weighs') and the book having a line for the dog and none for 'the other thing'.

The courier chain rendered: a tarred canvas sack lead-sealed with the Line's waystation mark, brought up by the ferryman's boy, cut and sorted aloud by Pike by name; nineteen pieces counted; Hesk's letter addressed only 'Cael. Past the Line.' and reaching him because the board is where names are kept.

Cael's response to the letter through procedure: read once, filed flat against the leather book, the roof question turned over against the ash and the meadow, the grandmother filed as 'a new fact about his own life arrived by ferry three weeks old' and not questioned.

The wall-sheet mechanism for a one-line move: Pike unpins the sheet one-handed, copies the whole thirteen lines fresh at the table, places the five names twelfth, writes the crew 'named by its mule' (from Chapter 2) thirteenth, and re-pins in the same four holes; the room's carters and a new crew of three watching the bare wall; the crew of three reading the stick, the arm, and the hands as a verdict.
state_change_proposals: Timeline: the chapter opens on the second morning after the ford (fifty-fifth day past the Line) at Thornwater; the grain moves and the unit leaves Thornwater on the fifth day after the ford (fifty-eighth); one night camped above the wash; Lowmarch reached on the SIXTIETH day past the Line, ten days after they left it. The ford's slip was read at Pike's plank about a week before; the saying is done at the book on the evening of the sixtieth day. Cael is eighteen.

Cael: nine fragments + anomaly, unchanged. No deployment this chapter (idle drift only: Shadow tried at the landing when the ferry came in; Anchor wants the inn door). Injury OPEN at chapter end: right calf, bitten through at the ford, walked on with a limp he catalogues in paces (eleven flat, nine uphill, twelve down); nobody has mentioned it; no healer. Hesk's first letter east received on the sixtieth day and filed in the satchel against the leather book; no reply written (the ferry goes west again in a month; no roof). New personal knowledge: his grandmother crossed the Line once on a trade run before he was born and said the roads were honest and the food wasn't — one sentence, not questioned, not expanded. Marks: fifty-eight earned, forty-eight in hand (Chapter 2's eighteen/ten plus the ford's forty). The unit still sleeps in the meadow, ten paces on from the ash.

Brom: Injury OPEN: right forearm, bound and re-bound (re-bound by the steading's woman on the third day after the ford; re-bound by Brom himself, Cael holding the end, at the road camp); closed along most of its length, still open at the wrist, 'clean' and 'not right'; carries nothing; the good (left) hand does everything. Asked Pike privately what the board pays a man with no Path; received 'Same as anyone. What'd he do?'; wrote it down on one of Pike's old slips and keeps it inside his shirt — the second person in his life he has written down (Rooke, B4, was the first). His want (worth without a number) answered by Pike's ledger; not stated by Brom as resolved.

Lira: Injury OPEN: right ankle, setting stiff and wrong for want of a healer — bends 'less, and later' than the other; walks on a stick (a cut-down hay-fork handle); rode the grain cart's tail on the road. Her want stated aloud at the fire, to the fire, not to Cael: 'So what am I becoming, exactly, if nobody's measuring?' — unanswered, and she does not ask it again. She has heard nothing about quiet ground beyond the carter's wife's three sentences (she was present in the barn, not the yard; the sentences were reported to nobody).

Karis: Injury OPEN: both palms cut, wrapped to the fingers; on the fifth day after the ford she can write with the pen pinned across the wrapped palm and the hand moving from the elbow; handwriting twice its size and leaning; she has noted the state in the notebook itself ('Hand poor. Fifth day after. Entries stand as written.') and has taken her notes back from Cael's dictation. The three boxes were opened as a working library on Thornwater's barn table and repacked for the road (the boxes now at the Lowmarch meadow). She holds the phrase 'quiet ground' from an unnamed carter's wife, written verbatim with 'everybody knows' underlined twice, filed as a source ('Not a good one. The first.'); she has NOT asked anyone about it, has not asked Pike, and knows nothing of what it is. She has one page of edge-territory lore (the ford lore) and no other primary source from this side of the Line.

Seln: uninjured. Has walked every road out of Lowmarch (in the four days before the ford) as he walked every road out of Thornwater, and told nobody until now. Took the four-mark well-clearing on the south road from the board (slip marked; not yet walked or done). Stated his want aloud at the board, unasked: 'I keep waiting for someone to ask for my report.' — and that he does not want to be asked; the craft is the same with the weight off. First honest employment continues.

Pike's ledger and wall: the ford's completion line said aloud at the book on the evening of the sixtieth day with the crew present ('That's said.'); the wall sheet at the lower inn rewritten by Pike in full and re-pinned with the five names TWELFTH of thirteen (one line up), the mule-named crew thirteenth, Teague's crew still first with ten names between. Pike's spoken count: 'Teague's still eleven up.' Pike's stated rule for Teague on record: 'He'll speak to you when you've cost him something. That's not rudeness. That's the ledger.' Pike on his own standing: Copper, thirty years on the roads, stopped carrying his paper in the second year.

Board state at Lowmarch, sixtieth day: fourteen slips (the ford clearance, the autumn-road walk — HOLD, Teague, sixty and fed, walked or being walked — and the thirty-mark grain escort all gone; two escorts, a fence-line, and a well-clearing at four marks added). Teague's crew absent from Lowmarch on the autumn road; the best table kept empty with a full jug. A new crew of three at the middle table (unnamed, uncatalogued beyond 'new faces, new canvas').

Courier chain established on the page: a monthly tarred mail sack, lead-sealed with the Line's waystation mark, carried by the ferry to the Line and back; sorted aloud by name at Pike's plank; nineteen pieces this month (eleven carters, four crews, three inns, one for Cael). The next westbound ferry is a month off.

Knowledge state: nobody in the party knows anything about quiet ground beyond the carter's wife's three sentences; nobody has seen it, asked Pike, or investigated. Healer shortage confirmed as a rationing fact in the steading's woman's words ('They stop inside, where the tiers are'); no healer, no Tide practitioner, no Oryn on the page.

Third-party verdicts on record this chapter: the steading's woman — 'It'll set how it sets.' / 'Healer would've had it straight in an hour.' / 'They stop inside, where the tiers are.'; Pike — 'Same as anyone. What'd he do?'; 'Held a dog with a shoulder and a river, that one. That's on a line in my book.'; the closing line. deviations: Word count 5,273 against a 4,600 target — inside the 15% tolerance (ceiling 5,290) but above target, in line with Chapters 1–3 (5,269 / 5,169 / 5,150). The first pass ran to 5,794 and was cut by density only; every mandated line, all four movements, all four injuries, the mid-chapter log, and the mandated ending are intact. Further compression toward 4,600 is available in the field-library catalogue, the road-camp texture, and the mail-sorting beat without touching obligations.

Ledger arithmetic: Chapter 2 placed the unit thirteenth with 'eleven lines between' them and Teague (twelve positions apart). After the one-line move mandated here they are twelfth with ten names between, and the card's fixed closing line says 'Teague's still eleven up.' The chapter renders both counts honestly — Cael counts 'Ten names between ... Twelfth. One line.' and Pike says 'eleven up' — treating Pike's phrase as the count of lines from the unit's line to Teague's (twelfth to first = eleven), which also matches Chapter 2's Pike agreeing 'Eleven' at the plank while the unit stood thirteenth. The editor may prefer a different reconciliation (e.g., a crew leaving the sheet); the prose does not assert one, and only the two counts are on the page.

'Eight weeks' is used (Karis, Seln) for the time past the Line at the sixtieth day. The Chapter 8 card's log line says 'Eight weeks' at a later date; that is an architecture-internal figure and was not treated as a constraint here, but the editor may want to reconcile the book's week-count language across Ch4/Ch8.

The card's 'Brom has done so for exactly two people in his life' is rendered as Cael's knowledge ('once before in his life that Cael knew of ... Rooke ... That made two'), to stay inside POV; the log states 'Second time in his life' flatly, as Cael's belief.

Hesk's letter is addressed on its outside only 'Cael. Past the Line.' — an invention to avoid implying an earlier letter from Cael naming Lowmarch (which the packet forbids as 'no other letters'); it reaches him because Pike sorts the sack by name. No fact about the Line's waystation beyond a lead seal and a monthly ferry is asserted.

The ford's completion line was already entered in Pike's book in Chapter 3 (copied to the crew by carter). This chapter honors the card's 'entering the ford in front of them' as the ledger's second reading — 'the saying' — done aloud with the crew present, consistent with Chapter 2's 'once before it's in ... once after, so it's said'; the wall-sheet move is staged as the on-page entry the card asks for.

The healer shortage is stated in the steading's woman's words ('They stop inside, where the tiers are') and Cael's filing, not as a Compact fact; no numbers, no Path named, no healer named. The Chapter 3 phrase 'walks a route' is echoed once in Cael's head as the woman's own count and not developed.
